Slides accessible here: `https://pengyunc.quarto.pub/week9/` ## This tutorial This tutorial uses lag polynomials to (A) understand and (B) extend our ARMA modelling approach.
:::{.callout-note title="Agenda"} - We will make use of `BAB3mth.csv` from Week 4 and `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1. - All code is provided in the questions in order to focus on the concepts and results. - Part A: Common factors in ARMA models (`BAB3mth.csv`) - Part B: Multiplicative models: seasonal autoregression (`RetailSales.csv`) :::
**Initialisation** for Part A ```{r} library(urca) library(forecast) dt <- read.csv("BAB3mth.csv") Y <- ts(dt$BAB3, start=c(2010,1), end=c(2025,6), frequency=12) DY <- diff(Y) Y <- window(Y, end=c(2024,6)) DY <- window(DY, end=c(2024,6)) ``` ## What's going on? {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} Estimating an AR model is computationally simple. - you can simply compute this by OLS (by matrix algebra, $\hat{\beta}=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}(X^{\top}y)$) ::: :::{.fragment} Estimating a model with an MA component is much more computationally intensive. - you need to rely on numerical methods (e.g. maximum likelihood) ::: :::{.fragment} :::{.callout-tip} Suppose we want to estimate the most basic ARMA(1,1). $$y_{t}=\phi_{1}y_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}$$ The maximum likelihood algorithm proceeds as follows: :::{.incremental} - First, guess $(\phi_{1},\theta_{1})$. - Next, plug these values into the model, and compute the implied residuals $U_{t}$. - Compute the likelihood function (how probable the observed data are given those parameters) - Repeat the process until the likelihood function is maximised. ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment}
However, with invertibility, the MA component can be approximated by AR models. ::: ## What's going on? {auto-animate="true"} However, with invertibility, the MA component can be approximated by AR models. :::{.fragment}
**What is invertibility?** MA is invertible $\to$ can be re-written as an AR($\infty$) representation (with converging coefficients) ::: :::{.fragment}
**Why can AR models approximate the MA component?** :::{.callout-tip title="Lecture Example: MA(1)"} $$\begin{aligned} Z_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\;\;\xrightarrow{\textsf{can be written as}}\;\;& Z_{t}=\sum^{\infty}_{j=1}-(-\theta_{1})^{j}Z_{t-j}+U_{t}\\ \textsf{or, when there is finite horizon:}\;\;& Z_{t}=\sum^{t-1}_{j=1}-(-\theta_{1})^{j}Z_{t-j}+U_{t}-(-\theta_{1})^{t}U_{0} \end{aligned}$$ :::
::: :::{.fragment} If $|\theta_{1}|<1$, then $(-\theta_{1})^{t}$ shrinks to 0 as $t$ becomes larger $\to$ ignoring certain higher-order AR terms can still yield a reasonable approximation. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} **Example:** In Tutorial 8, the optimal ARMA model for $\Delta Y_{t}$ is ARMA(1,2) with drift. \begin{align*} \Delta{}Y_{t}&=\beta_{0}+Z_{t}\\ Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2} \end{align*} :::{.fragment} Consider only the second equation. Moving all AR terms to the LHS gives: $$Z_{t}-\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Next, replace the notation with lag operators $L$, where $L^{n}(x_{t})=x_{t-n}$: $$Z_{t}-\phi_{1}L(Z_{t})=U_{t}+\theta_{1}L(U_{t})+\theta_{2}L^{2}(U_{t})$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$(1-\phi_{1}L)Z_{t}=\color{green}{\underbrace{(1+\theta_{1}L+\theta_{2}L^{2})}_{\substack{\textsf{the MA lag polynomial}\\\textsf{we are interested in}}}}\color{black}{U_{t}}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Compute the solution of the lag polynomial for the MA component: \begin{align*} 1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}&=0\\ \color{teal}{\boxed{\textsf{\small{}Suppose the solutions are $\to$}}}\qquad \zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}&=\frac{-\theta_{1}\pm\sqrt{\theta_{1}^{2}-4\theta_{2}}}{2\theta_{2}} \end{align*} ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} Compute the solution of the lag polynomial for the MA component: \begin{align*} 1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}&=0\\ \color{teal}{\boxed{\textsf{\small{}Suppose the solutions are $\to$}}}\qquad \zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}&=\frac{-\theta_{1}\pm\sqrt{\theta_{1}^{2}-4\theta_{2}}}{2\theta_{2}} \end{align*} :::{.fragment} This means that the lag polynomial can be rewritten as: $$(\zeta_{1}-z)(\zeta_{2}-z)=0$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\color{teal}{\zeta_{1}}\color{black}{(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}z)\,\times\,} \color{teal}{\zeta_{2}}\color{black}{(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}z)=0}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}z)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}z)=0$$ ::: :::{.fragment} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane.
:::{.fragment} **Aside.** Consider an ARMA(2,2) model: \begin{align*} (1-\phi_{1}L-\phi_{2}L^{2})Z_{t}&=(1+\theta_{1}L+\theta_{2}L^{2})U_{t}\\ (1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\xi_{2}^{-1}L)Z_{t}&=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)U_{t} \end{align*} where $\xi_{1}^{-1},\xi_{2}^{-1}$ are inverse roots of the AR lag polynomial: $1-\phi_{1}z-\phi_{2}z^{2}=0$.
::: :::{.fragment} The AR component is **stationary** if: $$|\xi_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad\text{and}\quad |\xi_{2}^{-1}|<1$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the AR lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. :::{.panel-tabset} ## Parameter Estimates ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) # ARMA(1,2) print(coef(eq)) ```
Thus the lag polynomial for the MA component is: \begin{align*} 1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}&=0\\ 1-0.3046z-0.3105z^{2}&=0 \end{align*} ## MA Inverse Roots The `polyroot()` function in R solves for the complex roots of a polynomial. (the coefficients has to be ordered from the constant term to the highest degree term) $$1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}=0$$ ```{r} MA2roots <- polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2")])) MA2invroots <- 1/MA2roots print(round(MA2invroots,4)) ```
So we have $\zeta_{1}^{-1}=0.7300$ and $\zeta_{2}^{-1}=-0.4254$. ## Checking Magnitude The magnitudes for these inverse roots (takes form $\zeta^{-1}=a+ib$) are: $$|\zeta^{-1}|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}} \quad\implies\quad\begin{aligned}|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|&=\sqrt{0.73^{2}+0^{2}}=0.73\;\color{green}{<1}\\ |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|&=\sqrt{(-0.4254)^{2}+0^{2}}=0.4254\;\color{green}{<1} \end{aligned}$$ The relevant R function is `Mod()`: ```{r} print(Mod(MA2invroots)) ```
Since both inverse roots are less than 1 in magnitude $\to$ lies within the unit circle. ## Plot ```{r} plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",1,",",2,") "), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ::: {.absolute top="650px" left="950px" style="font-size: 32px;"} $$\begin{aligned} &\textsf{Right panel:}\\ &\zeta_{1}^{-1}=0.7300\\ &\zeta_{2}^{-1}=-0.4254 \end{aligned}$$ ::: ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Progressively increment the orders of *both* AR and MA models so that we estimate ARMA(1,2), ARMA(2,3), ARMA(3,4) and ARMA(4,5) models. Plot the inverted roots for these four models. Discuss the implication of plots. :::
```{r eval = FALSE} for (j in 0:3){ eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1+j,0,2+j)) plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",1+j,",",2+j,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) } ``` :::{.panel-tabset} ## ARMA(1,2) ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) # ARMA(1,2) plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",1,",",2,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ## ARMA(2,3) ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(2,0,3)) # ARMA(2,3) plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",2,",",3,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ## ARMA(3,4) ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(3,0,4)) # ARMA(3,4) plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",3,",",4,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ## ARMA(4,5) ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(4,0,5)) # ARMA(4,5) plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",4,",",5,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.panel-tabset} ## ARMA(1,2) ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) MA2invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2")])) print(round(MA2invroots,4)) # MA Inverse roots print(round(Mod(MA2invroots),4)) # Magnitudes of MA inverse roots ``` ```{r echo=FALSE} plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",1,",",2,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ## ARMA(2,3) ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(2,0,3)) MA3invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2", "ma3")])) print(round(MA3invroots,4)) # MA Inverse roots print(round(Mod(MA3invroots),4)) # Magnitudes of MA inverse roots ``` ```{r echo=FALSE} plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",2,",",3,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ::: {.absolute top="470px" left="920px" style="font-size: 30px;"} Both extra inverted AR and MA roots are very close to 1 $\Rightarrow$ this model for the same time series apparently has suddenly become both non-stationary and non-invertible. ::: ::: {.absolute top="590px" left="128px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\swarrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="590px" left="610px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\swarrow$ ::: ## ARMA(3,4) ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(3,0,4)) MA4invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2", "ma3", "ma4")])) print(round(MA4invroots,4)) # MA inverse roots print(round(Mod(MA4invroots),4)) # Magnitudes of MA inverse roots ``` ```{r echo=FALSE} plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",3,",",4,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ::: {.absolute top="470px" left="920px" style="font-size: 30px;"} With the addition of 2 to both AR and MA orders, we now have two additional (very close to) non-stationary AR inverse roots and two non-invertible MA inverse roots, all four of which happen to be complex. ::: ::: {.absolute top="525px" left="290px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\nearrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="710px" left="290px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\searrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="525px" left="770px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\nearrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="710px" left="770px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\searrow$ ::: ## ARMA(4,5) ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(4,0,5)) MA5invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2", "ma3", "ma4", "ma5")])) print(round(MA5invroots,4)) # MA inverse roots print(round(Mod(MA5invroots),4)) # Magnitudes of MA inverse roots ``` ```{r echo=FALSE} plot(eq) mtext(paste0("ARMA(",4,",",5,")"), side=3, line=2, cex=1.3, font=2) ``` ::: {.absolute top="560px" left="920px" style="font-size: 30px;"} Now there are three additional (very close to) non-stationary AR inverse roots and non-invertible MA inverse roots. ::: ::: {.absolute top="560px" left="290px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\nearrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="740px" left="290px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\searrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="560px" left="770px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\nearrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="740px" left="770px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\searrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="620px" left="128px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\swarrow$ ::: ::: {.absolute top="620px" left="610px" style="font-size: 40px;"} $\swarrow$ ::: ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} **What is going on here?** ::: :::{.fragment} :::{.callout-note} In Tutorial 8, the optimal ARMA model for $\Delta Y_{t}$, chosen by the AICc, is ARMA(1,2). Let's assume that it is the correct model. :::
::: :::{.fragment} The AIC-selected ARMA(1,2) model can be written symbolically as: $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} The AR and MA inverse roots are: ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) MA2invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2")])) ARinvroots <- eq$coef[c("ar1")] mydata <- matrix(c(ARinvroots, MA2invroots), nrow=1) colnames(mydata) <- c("xi_1", "zeta_1", "zeta_2") rownames(mydata) <- c("") print(round(mydata,4)) ``` $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} If ARMA(1,2) is indeed the correct model, then if we increment the specification to ARMA(2,3), $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\color{purple}{\xi_{2}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)(1\,-}\color{teal}{\,\zeta_{3}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$ the “correct” values of the excess terms $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ should be 0. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} **What is going on here?** ::: $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$
If ARMA(1,2) is indeed the correct model, then if we increment the specification to ARMA(2,3), $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\color{purple}{\xi_{2}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)(1\,-}\color{teal}{\,\zeta_{3}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$ the “correct” values of the excess terms $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ should be 0. :::{.fragment}
Unfortunately things get more complicated in this specification. ::: :::{.fragment} The AR and MA inverse roots for ARMA(2,3) are: ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(2,0,3)) MA3invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2", "ma3")])) AR2invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,-eq$coef[c("ar1", "ar2")])) mydata <- matrix(c(AR2invroots, MA3invroots), nrow=1) colnames(mydata) <- c("xi_1", "xi_2", "zeta_1", "zeta_2", "zeta_3") rownames(mydata) <- c("") print(round(mydata,4)) ``` [$$(1-0.9092L)(1-\color{purple}{(-0.9885)}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-0.7477L)(1+0.4993L)(1-}\color{teal}{(-0.9564)}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$]{.small} where $\xi_{2}^{-1}=-0.9885$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}=-0.9564$ are very much not 0. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} **What is going on here?** ::: $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$ [$$(1-0.9092L)\color{red}{(1+0.9885L)}\color{black}{Z_{t}=(1-0.7477L)(1+0.4993L)}\color{red}{(1+0.9564L)}\color{black}{U_{t}}$$]{.small} By introducing the extra terms on both sides we have introduced what is referred to as a “common factor"[, and the "common factor" can be “cancelled” from both sides.]{.fragment} :::{.fragment}
What does this mean, and what is the problem? ::: :::{.incremental} - There is only one true data generating process in reality, indicating there is a unique set of AR and MA roots $(\xi_{1}^{-1},\xi_{2}^{-1},\zeta_{1}^{-1},\zeta_{2}^{-1},\zeta^{-1}_{3})$. [Therefore, there should only be a unique set of AR $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$ and MA $(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ parameters.]{.fragment} - Since the common factor can be cancelled out, the inverse roots $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ can now take on a range of values **as long as $\xi_{2}^{-1}=\zeta_{3}^{-1}$**. [$\implies$ the model parameters $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ are NOT unique]{.fragment} [$\implies$ the model is **NOT identified!**]{.fragment} - This is why the numerical algorithm pushes the excess parameters ($\xi_{2}^{-1}$, $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$) towards the unit circle, even though we might expect them to shrink towards zero. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} **Some practical observations:** :::{.incremental} - If an ARMA($p,q$) model has inverse roots that nearly cancel, especially near the unit circle, you should reconsider whether smaller orders would suffice. - As AIC/AICc is balancing between model complexity and fit quality, it would usually be the case that it will work to avoid this issue. - However, it is worth acknowledging that AICc is not perfect and might select models that is too large. - When doing model selection searches, it is generally advised to avoid increasing the order of both AR and MA components simultaneously. - It is better to increase AR or MA components separately, in which case this potential identification problem should be avoided. - Brute-force AIC search over ($p,q$) works for small grids but can cause instability at larger orders $\to$ there exists smarter methods (e.g. `auto.arima`) avoid this. - More pragmatically, at least in economics and finance it has become more common to rely simply on AR models rather than ARMA. - Avoids the common factor problem, quicker (can use OLS), more stable than ARMA, and simplifies extensions to multivariate models (e.g. VAR). ::: ## Part B: Multiplicative Models: Seasonal Autoregression {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} An alternative model for seasonality is the seasonal AR model. (There is also a seasonal MA model, which follows the same principles.) ::: :::{.fragment}
A simple example is the first order seasonal AR (SAR) model, specified here for quarterly data: $$ Z_{t}=\Phi_{1}Z_{t-4}+U_{t}\quad \iff\quad (1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t} $$ That is, $Y_{t}$ is modeled directly in terms of the observation from one year ago. This is four time periods for quarterly data, hence the $Z_{t-4}$ term. ::: :::{.fragment}
In general we can have higher order seasonal AR models: $$ (1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t} $$ which expresses the forecasts for $Y_{t}$ in terms of observations from $1,\dots,P$ years ago. ::: ## Part B: Multiplicative Models: Seasonal Autoregression {auto-animate="true"} Most commonly the SAR model is combined with an AR model, so that seasonal and non-seasonal components are permitted. :::{.fragment}
This is done in a multiplicative manner using lag polynomials. For example an AR(1),SAR(1) model is $$(1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ This is essentially a restricted AR(5) model. $\to$ Exercise 2(a) ::: :::{.fragment}
In general an AR($p$),SAR($P$) model is $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ The selection of $p$ and $P$ can be handled in the usual way using AIC and residual autcorrelation checks with Ljung-Box testing. ::: ## Exercise 2(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Expand the lag polynomials in the AR(1),SAR(1) model to show that it is equivalent to an AR(5) model with particular parameter restrictions. $$(1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ :::
:::{.fragment} We can algebraically manipulate lag polynomials like any other polynomial: \begin{align} (1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})&=1-\phi_{1}-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L\cdot L^{4}\\ &=1-\phi_{1}-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L^{5} \end{align} ::: :::{.fragment} Thus the model can be re-written as: $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L^{5})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\qquad Z_{t}=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\Phi_{1}Z_{t-4}-\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}Z_{t-5}+U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Comparing this model with the standard AR(5) setup: $$Z_{t}=\phi_{1}^* Z_{t-1}+\phi_{2}^* Z_{t-2}+\phi_{3}^* Z_{t-3}+\phi_{4}^* Z_{t-4}+\phi_{5}^* Z_{t-5}+U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} the restrictions are $\phi_{1}^*=\phi_{1}$, $\phi_{2}=\phi_{3}=0$, $\phi_{4}^{*}=\Phi_{1}$ and $\phi_{5}^*=-\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}$. :::
## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Using `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1/2, carry out a model selection search over AR($p$), SAR($P$) models with maximum of 4 for both $p$ and $P$. $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ What is the longest lag of $Z_{t}$ implied by this AR,SAR model? :::
**Initialisation:** Copy the following to set up in the usual way ```{r} library(forecast) # Set up log retail sales, 2000q1 to 2019q4 dt <- read.csv("RetailSales.csv") Retail_m <- ts(dt$Total, frequency=12, start=c(1982,4), end=c(2024,9)) Retail_q <- aggregate(Retail_m, nfrequency=4) log_Retail_q <- log(Retail_q) Y <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2019,4)) # Linear trend Time <- time(Y) ```
(continued next slide...) ## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} Set up deterministics: ```{r} # GFC trend break gfc <- 2008.5 Time_postgfc <- 1*(Time>gfc)*(Time-gfc) # Quarterly dummies QD <- seasonaldummy(Y) # Deterministics without seasonal dummies X <- cbind(Time, Time_postgfc) # Deterministics with seasonal dummies XQD <- cbind(Time, Time_postgfc, QD) ```
Define samples for estimation and forecast evaluation: ```{r} # Estimation sample t_est <- which(Time<2019) Y <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4)) # Forecast evaluation sample t_for <- which(Time>=2019) Yf <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2019,1), end=c(2019,4)) ``` ## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Using `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1/2, carry out a model selection search over AR($p$), SAR($P$) models with maximum of 4 for both $p$ and $P$. $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ What is the longest lag of $Z_{t}$ implied by this AR,SAR model? :::
```{r} pmax <- 4 Pmax <- 4 AICc <- matrix(nrow=1+pmax, ncol=1+Pmax) rownames(AICc) <- paste0("AR",0:pmax) colnames(AICc) <- paste0("SAR",0:Pmax) LBp <- AICc for (p in 0:pmax){ for (P in 0:Pmax){ # Specification of AR(p), SAR(P) model: eq_sar <- Arima(Y, order=c(p,0,0), xreg=X[t_est,], seasonal=list(order=c(P,0,0), period=4)) AICc[1+p,1+P] <- eq_sar$aicc LBp[1+p,1+P] <- Box.test(eq_sar$residuals, type="Ljung-Box", fitdf=p+P, lag=12)$p.value } } ```

:::{.callout-note title="Agenda"} - We will make use of `BAB3mth.csv` from Week 4 and `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1. - All code is provided in the questions in order to focus on the concepts and results. - Part A: Common factors in ARMA models (`BAB3mth.csv`) - Part B: Multiplicative models: seasonal autoregression (`RetailSales.csv`) :::
**Initialisation** for Part A ```{r} library(urca) library(forecast) dt <- read.csv("BAB3mth.csv") Y <- ts(dt$BAB3, start=c(2010,1), end=c(2025,6), frequency=12) DY <- diff(Y) Y <- window(Y, end=c(2024,6)) DY <- window(DY, end=c(2024,6)) ``` ## What's going on? {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} Estimating an AR model is computationally simple. - you can simply compute this by OLS (by matrix algebra, $\hat{\beta}=(X^{\top}X)^{-1}(X^{\top}y)$) ::: :::{.fragment} Estimating a model with an MA component is much more computationally intensive. - you need to rely on numerical methods (e.g. maximum likelihood) ::: :::{.fragment} :::{.callout-tip} Suppose we want to estimate the most basic ARMA(1,1). $$y_{t}=\phi_{1}y_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}$$ The maximum likelihood algorithm proceeds as follows: :::{.incremental} - First, guess $(\phi_{1},\theta_{1})$. - Next, plug these values into the model, and compute the implied residuals $U_{t}$. - Compute the likelihood function (how probable the observed data are given those parameters) - Repeat the process until the likelihood function is maximised. ::: ::: ::: :::{.fragment}
However, with invertibility, the MA component can be approximated by AR models. ::: ## What's going on? {auto-animate="true"} However, with invertibility, the MA component can be approximated by AR models. :::{.fragment}
**What is invertibility?** MA is invertible $\to$ can be re-written as an AR($\infty$) representation (with converging coefficients) ::: :::{.fragment}
**Why can AR models approximate the MA component?** :::{.callout-tip title="Lecture Example: MA(1)"} $$\begin{aligned} Z_{t}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}\;\;\xrightarrow{\textsf{can be written as}}\;\;& Z_{t}=\sum^{\infty}_{j=1}-(-\theta_{1})^{j}Z_{t-j}+U_{t}\\ \textsf{or, when there is finite horizon:}\;\;& Z_{t}=\sum^{t-1}_{j=1}-(-\theta_{1})^{j}Z_{t-j}+U_{t}-(-\theta_{1})^{t}U_{0} \end{aligned}$$ :::
::: :::{.fragment} If $|\theta_{1}|<1$, then $(-\theta_{1})^{t}$ shrinks to 0 as $t$ becomes larger $\to$ ignoring certain higher-order AR terms can still yield a reasonable approximation. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} **Example:** In Tutorial 8, the optimal ARMA model for $\Delta Y_{t}$ is ARMA(1,2) with drift. \begin{align*} \Delta{}Y_{t}&=\beta_{0}+Z_{t}\\ Z_{t}&=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2} \end{align*} :::{.fragment} Consider only the second equation. Moving all AR terms to the LHS gives: $$Z_{t}-\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}=U_{t}+\theta_{1}U_{t-1}+\theta_{2}U_{t-2}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Next, replace the notation with lag operators $L$, where $L^{n}(x_{t})=x_{t-n}$: $$Z_{t}-\phi_{1}L(Z_{t})=U_{t}+\theta_{1}L(U_{t})+\theta_{2}L^{2}(U_{t})$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$(1-\phi_{1}L)Z_{t}=\color{green}{\underbrace{(1+\theta_{1}L+\theta_{2}L^{2})}_{\substack{\textsf{the MA lag polynomial}\\\textsf{we are interested in}}}}\color{black}{U_{t}}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Compute the solution of the lag polynomial for the MA component: \begin{align*} 1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}&=0\\ \color{teal}{\boxed{\textsf{\small{}Suppose the solutions are $\to$}}}\qquad \zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}&=\frac{-\theta_{1}\pm\sqrt{\theta_{1}^{2}-4\theta_{2}}}{2\theta_{2}} \end{align*} ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} Compute the solution of the lag polynomial for the MA component: \begin{align*} 1+\theta_{1}z+\theta_{2}z^{2}&=0\\ \color{teal}{\boxed{\textsf{\small{}Suppose the solutions are $\to$}}}\qquad \zeta_{1},\zeta_{2}&=\frac{-\theta_{1}\pm\sqrt{\theta_{1}^{2}-4\theta_{2}}}{2\theta_{2}} \end{align*} :::{.fragment} This means that the lag polynomial can be rewritten as: $$(\zeta_{1}-z)(\zeta_{2}-z)=0$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$\color{teal}{\zeta_{1}}\color{black}{(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}z)\,\times\,} \color{teal}{\zeta_{2}}\color{black}{(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}z)=0}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} $$(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}z)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}z)=0$$ ::: :::{.fragment} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane.
:::{.fragment} **Aside.** Consider an ARMA(2,2) model: \begin{align*} (1-\phi_{1}L-\phi_{2}L^{2})Z_{t}&=(1+\theta_{1}L+\theta_{2}L^{2})U_{t}\\ (1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\xi_{2}^{-1}L)Z_{t}&=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)U_{t} \end{align*} where $\xi_{1}^{-1},\xi_{2}^{-1}$ are inverse roots of the AR lag polynomial: $1-\phi_{1}z-\phi_{2}z^{2}=0$.
::: :::{.fragment} The AR component is **stationary** if: $$|\xi_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad\text{and}\quad |\xi_{2}^{-1}|<1$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the AR lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. ::: ## What makes an MA model invertible? {auto-animate="true"} The MA component is **invertible** if: $$|\zeta_{1}^{-1}|<1\quad \text{and}\quad |\zeta_{2}^{-1}|<1.$$ Graphically, the inverse roots of the MA lag polynomial should lie **within** the unit circle in the Real-Imaginary plane. :::{.panel-tabset} ## Parameter Estimates ```{r} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) # ARMA(1,2) print(coef(eq)) ```

Let's assume that it is the correct model. :::
::: :::{.fragment} The AIC-selected ARMA(1,2) model can be written symbolically as: $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} The AR and MA inverse roots are: ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(1,0,2)) MA2invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2")])) ARinvroots <- eq$coef[c("ar1")] mydata <- matrix(c(ARinvroots, MA2invroots), nrow=1) colnames(mydata) <- c("xi_1", "zeta_1", "zeta_2") rownames(mydata) <- c("") print(round(mydata,4)) ``` $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} If ARMA(1,2) is indeed the correct model, then if we increment the specification to ARMA(2,3), $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\color{purple}{\xi_{2}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)(1\,-}\color{teal}{\,\zeta_{3}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$ the “correct” values of the excess terms $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ should be 0. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} **What is going on here?** ::: $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$
If ARMA(1,2) is indeed the correct model, then if we increment the specification to ARMA(2,3), $$(1-\xi_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\color{purple}{\xi_{2}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-\zeta_{1}^{-1}L)(1-\zeta_{2}^{-1}L)(1\,-}\color{teal}{\,\zeta_{3}^{-1}}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$ the “correct” values of the excess terms $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ should be 0. :::{.fragment}
Unfortunately things get more complicated in this specification. ::: :::{.fragment} The AR and MA inverse roots for ARMA(2,3) are: ```{r echo=FALSE} eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(2,0,3)) MA3invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,eq$coef[c("ma1", "ma2", "ma3")])) AR2invroots <- 1/polyroot(c(1,-eq$coef[c("ar1", "ar2")])) mydata <- matrix(c(AR2invroots, MA3invroots), nrow=1) colnames(mydata) <- c("xi_1", "xi_2", "zeta_1", "zeta_2", "zeta_3") rownames(mydata) <- c("") print(round(mydata,4)) ``` [$$(1-0.9092L)(1-\color{purple}{(-0.9885)}\color{black}{L)Z_{t}=(1-0.7477L)(1+0.4993L)(1-}\color{teal}{(-0.9564)}\color{black}{L)U_{t}}$$]{.small} where $\xi_{2}^{-1}=-0.9885$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}=-0.9564$ are very much not 0. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} **What is going on here?** ::: $$(1-0.9038L)Z_{t}=(1-0.73L)(1+0.4254L)U_{t}$$ [$$(1-0.9092L)\color{red}{(1+0.9885L)}\color{black}{Z_{t}=(1-0.7477L)(1+0.4993L)}\color{red}{(1+0.9564L)}\color{black}{U_{t}}$$]{.small} By introducing the extra terms on both sides we have introduced what is referred to as a “common factor"[, and the "common factor" can be “cancelled” from both sides.]{.fragment} :::{.fragment}
What does this mean, and what is the problem? ::: :::{.incremental} - There is only one true data generating process in reality, indicating there is a unique set of AR and MA roots $(\xi_{1}^{-1},\xi_{2}^{-1},\zeta_{1}^{-1},\zeta_{2}^{-1},\zeta^{-1}_{3})$. [Therefore, there should only be a unique set of AR $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})$ and MA $(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ parameters.]{.fragment} - Since the common factor can be cancelled out, the inverse roots $\xi_{2}^{-1}$ and $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$ can now take on a range of values **as long as $\xi_{2}^{-1}=\zeta_{3}^{-1}$**. [$\implies$ the model parameters $(\phi_{1},\phi_{2},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})$ are NOT unique]{.fragment} [$\implies$ the model is **NOT identified!**]{.fragment} - This is why the numerical algorithm pushes the excess parameters ($\xi_{2}^{-1}$, $\zeta_{3}^{-1}$) towards the unit circle, even though we might expect them to shrink towards zero. ::: ## Part A: Common factors in ARMA models {auto-animate="true"} **Some practical observations:** :::{.incremental} - If an ARMA($p,q$) model has inverse roots that nearly cancel, especially near the unit circle, you should reconsider whether smaller orders would suffice. - As AIC/AICc is balancing between model complexity and fit quality, it would usually be the case that it will work to avoid this issue. - However, it is worth acknowledging that AICc is not perfect and might select models that is too large. - When doing model selection searches, it is generally advised to avoid increasing the order of both AR and MA components simultaneously. - It is better to increase AR or MA components separately, in which case this potential identification problem should be avoided. - Brute-force AIC search over ($p,q$) works for small grids but can cause instability at larger orders $\to$ there exists smarter methods (e.g. `auto.arima`) avoid this. - More pragmatically, at least in economics and finance it has become more common to rely simply on AR models rather than ARMA. - Avoids the common factor problem, quicker (can use OLS), more stable than ARMA, and simplifies extensions to multivariate models (e.g. VAR). ::: ## Part B: Multiplicative Models: Seasonal Autoregression {auto-animate="true"} :::{.fragment} An alternative model for seasonality is the seasonal AR model. (There is also a seasonal MA model, which follows the same principles.) ::: :::{.fragment}
A simple example is the first order seasonal AR (SAR) model, specified here for quarterly data: $$ Z_{t}=\Phi_{1}Z_{t-4}+U_{t}\quad \iff\quad (1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t} $$ That is, $Y_{t}$ is modeled directly in terms of the observation from one year ago. This is four time periods for quarterly data, hence the $Z_{t-4}$ term. ::: :::{.fragment}
In general we can have higher order seasonal AR models: $$ (1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t} $$ which expresses the forecasts for $Y_{t}$ in terms of observations from $1,\dots,P$ years ago. ::: ## Part B: Multiplicative Models: Seasonal Autoregression {auto-animate="true"} Most commonly the SAR model is combined with an AR model, so that seasonal and non-seasonal components are permitted. :::{.fragment}
This is done in a multiplicative manner using lag polynomials. For example an AR(1),SAR(1) model is $$(1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ This is essentially a restricted AR(5) model. $\to$ Exercise 2(a) ::: :::{.fragment}
In general an AR($p$),SAR($P$) model is $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ The selection of $p$ and $P$ can be handled in the usual way using AIC and residual autcorrelation checks with Ljung-Box testing. ::: ## Exercise 2(a) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Expand the lag polynomials in the AR(1),SAR(1) model to show that it is equivalent to an AR(5) model with particular parameter restrictions. $$(1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ :::
:::{.fragment} We can algebraically manipulate lag polynomials like any other polynomial: \begin{align} (1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4})&=1-\phi_{1}-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L\cdot L^{4}\\ &=1-\phi_{1}-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L^{5} \end{align} ::: :::{.fragment} Thus the model can be re-written as: $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\Phi_{1}L^{4}+\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}L^{5})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} $$\implies\qquad Z_{t}=\phi_{1}Z_{t-1}+\Phi_{1}Z_{t-4}-\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}Z_{t-5}+U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} Comparing this model with the standard AR(5) setup: $$Z_{t}=\phi_{1}^* Z_{t-1}+\phi_{2}^* Z_{t-2}+\phi_{3}^* Z_{t-3}+\phi_{4}^* Z_{t-4}+\phi_{5}^* Z_{t-5}+U_{t}$$ ::: :::{.fragment} the restrictions are $\phi_{1}^*=\phi_{1}$, $\phi_{2}=\phi_{3}=0$, $\phi_{4}^{*}=\Phi_{1}$ and $\phi_{5}^*=-\phi_{1}\Phi_{1}$. :::
## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Using `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1/2, carry out a model selection search over AR($p$), SAR($P$) models with maximum of 4 for both $p$ and $P$. $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ What is the longest lag of $Z_{t}$ implied by this AR,SAR model? :::
**Initialisation:** Copy the following to set up in the usual way ```{r} library(forecast) # Set up log retail sales, 2000q1 to 2019q4 dt <- read.csv("RetailSales.csv") Retail_m <- ts(dt$Total, frequency=12, start=c(1982,4), end=c(2024,9)) Retail_q <- aggregate(Retail_m, nfrequency=4) log_Retail_q <- log(Retail_q) Y <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2019,4)) # Linear trend Time <- time(Y) ```
(continued next slide...) ## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} Set up deterministics: ```{r} # GFC trend break gfc <- 2008.5 Time_postgfc <- 1*(Time>gfc)*(Time-gfc) # Quarterly dummies QD <- seasonaldummy(Y) # Deterministics without seasonal dummies X <- cbind(Time, Time_postgfc) # Deterministics with seasonal dummies XQD <- cbind(Time, Time_postgfc, QD) ```
Define samples for estimation and forecast evaluation: ```{r} # Estimation sample t_est <- which(Time<2019) Y <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4)) # Forecast evaluation sample t_for <- which(Time>=2019) Yf <- window(log_Retail_q, start=c(2019,1), end=c(2019,4)) ``` ## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Using `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1/2, carry out a model selection search over AR($p$), SAR($P$) models with maximum of 4 for both $p$ and $P$. $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ What is the longest lag of $Z_{t}$ implied by this AR,SAR model? :::
```{r} pmax <- 4 Pmax <- 4 AICc <- matrix(nrow=1+pmax, ncol=1+Pmax) rownames(AICc) <- paste0("AR",0:pmax) colnames(AICc) <- paste0("SAR",0:Pmax) LBp <- AICc for (p in 0:pmax){ for (P in 0:Pmax){ # Specification of AR(p), SAR(P) model: eq_sar <- Arima(Y, order=c(p,0,0), xreg=X[t_est,], seasonal=list(order=c(P,0,0), period=4)) AICc[1+p,1+P] <- eq_sar$aicc LBp[1+p,1+P] <- Box.test(eq_sar$residuals, type="Ljung-Box", fitdf=p+P, lag=12)$p.value } } ```
## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Using `RetailSales.csv` from Week 1/2, carry out a model selection search over AR($p$), SAR($P$) models with maximum of 4 for both $p$ and $P$. $$(1-\phi_{1}L-\cdots-\phi_{p}L^{p})(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\cdots-\Phi_{P}L^{4P})Z_{t}=U_{t}$$ What is the longest lag of $Z_{t}$ implied by this AR,SAR model? :::
**Results:** :::{.panel-tabset} ## AICc values ```{r} print(round(AICc, 4)) ``` ## Model selection search ```{r} print(AICc==min(AICc)) ```
The selected model has $p=1$ and $P=3$. $\implies$ longest lag of $Z_{t}$ is 13. $$\color{teal}{\boxed{\textsf{\small\;found by expanding this }\to\;}}\quad\color{black}{ (1-\phi_{1}L)(1-\Phi_{1}L^{4}-\Phi_{2}L^{8}-\Phi_{3}L^{12})Z_{t}=U_{t}}$$ ## Residual autocorrelation :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{r} print(round(LBp,3)) ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{r} print(1*(LBp<0.05)) ``` ::: ::::
Since $p=0.739>0.05$, we can maintain $H_0$ of no residual autocorrelation $\implies$ the AR(1),SAR(3) model is not misspecified. ::: ## Exercise 2(b) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Use the a model with the selected $p$ and $q$ to forecast the four quarters of 2019 (i.e. 1,2,3,4-steps ahead), and compute their RMSE. :::

The RMSE for AR(1),SAR(3) forecasts is: ```{r} print(RMSE_sar) ``` ## Exercise 2(c) {auto-animate="true"} :::{.callout-question} Previously we have identifed an AR(3) model is suitable when also using a linear trend with GFC break and quarterly dummies.
